title: Programming with Scratch
summary: Your first programming language: building scripts from blocks in Scratch, with events, sequence, coordinates, loops, selection, variables, broadcasts, My Blocks and simulations, then planning, building and testing your own game.
learn: The Scratch window: stage, sprites, blocks palette and scripts area
Events and sequence, motion and x/y coordinates, costumes and animation
Loops (iteration) and if/if-else (selection) with sensing blocks
Variables, data types (number, text, true/false) and operators
Broadcasts, and abstraction with My Blocks and inputs (a bridge to functions and parameters)
Simulations: how changing a variable in a model changes the outcome
Debugging, and developing a game for a real user in cycles of plan, develop, test and refine (new NI curriculum links S1, S4, S7, C1, C3, C4)
intro: Scratch is where many programmers start: you snap blocks together instead of typing code, but the ideas are the same ones you will use in C# later. In this topic you will learn the Scratch window, events, coordinates, animation, loops, decisions, variables, messages and your own custom blocks, build a simulation, and then plan, build, test and refine a game for a real user.

pages.spec: Describe what Scratch is and identify the stage, sprites, blocks palette and scripts area
pages.summary: Scratch is a free, block-based programming language: you snap blocks together into scripts instead of typing code. The Scratch window has a stage where things happen, sprites that you program, a blocks palette to choose blocks from and a scripts area to build them in.

blocks.text: **[[Scratch]]** is a free programming language made for beginners. Instead of typing code, you **drag and snap coloured blocks together**, a bit like LEGO. Each block is one instruction, so you never have to worry about spelling a command wrong or forgetting a semicolon.

Scratch was created by the **Lifelong Kindergarten group at the MIT Media Lab** in the USA and was first released in **2007**. Millions of young people use it around the world. You can use it free in a web browser at **scratch.mit.edu**, or download the Scratch app to use offline.
Why start with Scratch?

items: **No typing errors**: blocks only fit together in ways that make sense.
**You see results straight away**: click the green flag and your sprites move.
**Real programming ideas**: [[sequence]], [[selection]], [[iteration|Loop]] and [[variables|Variable]] are exactly the same ideas you will use later in C# at GCSE.
**Creative**: you can make games, animations, stories and quizzes.

Blocks that give a value are written in round brackets, like **(x position)**, and true/false blocks in angle brackets, like **<key (space) pressed?>**.

blocks.context: Niamh is making a Scratch project about Enniskillen Castle. Name the part of Scratch she uses for each job: (a) a photo of the castle behind everything; (b) a knight character who walks around; (c) the place she joins blocks together.
steps: (a) A background picture for the stage is a **backdrop**.
(b) A character she can program is a **sprite**.

blocks.text: A common mistake is building a script on the **wrong sprite**. If your cat will not move, check which sprite is highlighted in the sprite list: you may have built the script on the stage or on another sprite by accident.

Scratch saves projects online if you are logged in to an account. Your teacher may ask you to use **File > Save to your computer** instead, which saves an **.sb3** file you can load again next lesson.

pages.spec: Use event blocks to start scripts and explain why the sequence of blocks matters
pages.summary: Event (hat) blocks such as [when green flag clicked] or [when (space) key pressed] start a script. The blocks underneath then run in sequence, one after another from top to bottom, so putting them in the wrong order changes what happens.

diagram.title: Running a script in sequence
diagram.caption: Click each block. The script starts when its event happens, then runs from top to bottom.

nodes.label: when green flag clicked
nodes.detail: A hat block from Events. Nothing happens until the green flag is clicked.

nodes.detail: Puts the sprite back in the centre of the stage, so it starts in the same place every time.

nodes.detail: Shows a speech bubble. The script waits here for 2 seconds before moving on.

blocks.text: A program is a set of instructions. In Scratch, the instructions in a script do nothing until something **starts** them. That something is an **[[event]]**: clicking the green flag, pressing a key, clicking on a sprite or receiving a message.
Event blocks (hat blocks)
Event blocks are yellow and have a curved top, so nothing can go above them. That is why they are called **hat blocks**: they sit on top of a script like a hat.

head: Event block
The script starts when...
rows: the green flag above the stage is clicked. Used to start the whole project.
that key is pressed. You can choose any key, e.g. the right arrow.
someone clicks on the sprite with the mouse.
the stage changes to that backdrop.
a message is broadcast (see the page on broadcasts).
blocks.caption: Common event blocks

blocks.text: One sprite can have **several scripts**, each with its own hat block. For example, one script for the green flag and another for when the space key is pressed. They can even run at the same time.
Sequence: order matters

**[[Sequence]]** means instructions are carried out **one after another, in order**. A Scratch script always runs from the **top block down to the bottom block**. Change the order and you change the result.

blocks.title: Script A: a greeting
blocks.code:
[when green flag clicked]
[say (Welcome to Fermanagh!) for (2) seconds]
[move (100) steps]
[say (Mind the lough!) for (2) seconds]
blocks.output: The sprite speaks, then moves 100 steps, then speaks again.

blocks.title: Worked example: does the order matter?
blocks.context: Ryan wants his sprite to walk to the right and then say 'I made it!'. He builds: [when green flag clicked], [say (I made it!) for (2) seconds], [move (150) steps]. What goes wrong and how should he fix it?
steps: Scratch runs the blocks from top to bottom.
So the sprite says 'I made it!' **before** it has moved anywhere.
Fix: swap the two blocks so that [move (150) steps] comes **before** the say block.
blocks.answer: The speech happens too early. Moving the [move (150) steps] block above the say block puts the sequence right.

blocks.text: Say versus say for 2 seconds

head: [say (Hi!)]
[say (Hi!) for (2) seconds]
rows: Until another say block replaces it
No: the next block runs straight away
Yes: the next block waits for 2 seconds
A message that stays on screen
A conversation where things happen in turn

blocks.text: Computers are **very fast**. If you put [move (10) steps] four times in a row with nothing between them, it looks like one big jump. Add [wait (0.5) seconds] between blocks if you want to see each step happen.

Always start your green flag script with blocks that **reset** things, such as [go to x: (0) y: (0)] and [point in direction (90)]. Then the project starts the same way every time you click the green flag.
In the Computational Thinking topic you met **sequence** in flowcharts and algorithms. A Scratch script is just an algorithm written in blocks.

blocks.title: Key points
items: An event is something that happens, such as a click or key press, that starts a script.
Event blocks are hat blocks: they always go at the top of a script.
Sequence means blocks run one after another, from top to bottom.
Changing the order of blocks changes what the program does.
Use wait blocks or 'for 2 seconds' blocks so the user can see each step.

pages.spec: Use motion blocks and x and y coordinates to position and move a sprite on the stage
pages.summary: The stage is a grid 480 steps wide (x from -240 to 240) and 360 steps tall (y from -180 to 180), with (0, 0) in the centre. Motion blocks either move a sprite relative to where it is, such as [change x by (10)], or send it to an exact position, such as [go to x: (100) y: (50)].

diagram.title: Where is the sprite?
diagram.caption: Work out each answer, then click the hidden cell to check.
head: Question
Answer

blocks.text: To move a sprite to an exact spot, Scratch uses **[[coordinates|Coordinates]]**, just like the grids you use in maths. Every point on the stage has an **x coordinate** (how far left or right) and a **y coordinate** (how far up or down).
The stage is a grid

head: x (left and right)
y (up and down)
blocks.caption: The Scratch stage: 480 steps wide and 360 steps tall

blocks.text: Remember: **x comes first, then y**, written (x, y). A handy way to remember: you walk along the corridor (x) *before* you go up the stairs (y).

When you move the mouse over the stage in some versions of Scratch, the x and y position of the mouse pointer is shown. The **sprite info** panel under the stage also shows the selected sprite's x and y.
Two kinds of motion block

head: Moves relative to where the sprite is
Goes to an exact position
rows: [go to x: (0) y: (0)], [set x to (100)], [set y to (-50)], [glide (1) secs to x: () y: ()]
where the sprite is now (and its direction)
nothing: it always ends up in the same place

blocks.text: [move (10) steps] moves the sprite 10 steps **in the direction it is facing**. One step is one unit on the coordinate grid. [turn ↻ (15) degrees] turns it clockwise (to the right) and [turn ↺ (15) degrees] turns it anticlockwise (to the left).

blocks.title: Worked example 1: change x and change y
blocks.context: A sprite starts at (40, -30). These blocks run in order: [change x by (60)], [change y by (50)], [change x by (-120)]. Where does it finish?
steps: Start: x = 40, y = -30.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: move and turn
blocks.context: A sprite is at (0, 0), facing right (direction 90). It runs: [move (80) steps], [turn ↻ (90) degrees], [move (50) steps]. Where does it finish?
steps: Facing right, moving 80 steps adds 80 to x: position **(80, 0)**.
Turning 90 degrees clockwise from right makes it face **down** (direction 180).
Moving 50 steps down takes 50 off y: position **(80, -50)**.
blocks.answer: The sprite finishes at (80, -50), facing down.

blocks.text: Mixing up **set** and **change** is a very common bug. [set x to (10)] puts the sprite *at* x = 10. [change x by (10)] moves it *10 more* to the right. If your sprite jumps to the same spot every time instead of moving along, you have used set where you needed change.
Do not mix up x and y. [change y by (10)] moves a sprite **up**, not right. To fall down the screen, use a **negative** number: [change y by (-5)].

[if on edge, bounce] turns the sprite around when it touches the edge of the stage. Scratch also stops sprites from disappearing completely off the edge, so [set x to (500)] leaves the sprite just poking in at the right-hand edge rather than at x = 500.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The stage runs from x = -240 to 240 and y = -180 to 180; the centre is (0, 0).
Coordinates are written (x, y): x across, then y up or down.
Change blocks move a sprite relative to where it is; go to and set blocks send it to an exact place.
[move () steps] goes the way the sprite is facing; direction 90 is right, 0 is up.
Negative y is below the centre, negative x is left of the centre.

[turn ↻ (90) degrees]

Up

check.q: A sprite at (0, 0) faces right and runs [move (60) steps] then [turn ↻ (90) degrees] then [move (30) steps]. Where does it end?

Explain the difference between [set x to (50)] and [change x by (50)].
practice.a: Set puts the sprite at the exact position x = 50 wherever it was (1). Change adds 50 to its current x, moving it 50 steps right from where it is (1).

pages.spec: Use looks and sound blocks, and switch costumes to animate a sprite
pages.summary: Looks blocks change how a sprite appears: speech bubbles, size, effects, show and hide, and its costume. Switching quickly between costumes with a short wait in between makes an animation, just like a flip book, and sound blocks add music and effects.

diagram.title: How a walking animation works
diagram.caption: The loop repeats, so the sprite keeps switching costumes and looks as if it is walking.

items.label: Show costume 1
items.detail: The cat with its legs together.

items.label: Move a few steps
items.detail: [move (10) steps] carries the sprite a little way across the stage.

items.label: Wait a moment
items.detail: [wait (0.2) seconds] so your eyes can see this costume before it changes.

items.label: Next costume
items.detail: [next costume] swaps to costume 2: legs apart. After the last costume it goes back to the first.

blocks.text: A **[[costume]]** is one of the pictures a sprite can show. The Scratch Cat has two costumes: one with its legs together and one with its legs apart. You can see, draw and edit costumes in the **Costumes** tab.
Animation: a digital flip book

**Animation** is the trick of showing slightly different pictures one after another so quickly that it looks like movement. Cartoons and films work in exactly the same way. In Scratch you animate by switching costumes inside a loop.

blocks.title: A walking cat
blocks.code:
[when green flag clicked]
[forever]
    [move (10) steps]
    [next costume]
    [wait (0.2) seconds]
    [if on edge, bounce]
blocks.output: The cat walks from side to side, swapping costumes so its legs move.

blocks.text: Without the [wait (0.2) seconds] block, the costumes change so fast that the animation is a blur. Too long a wait (e.g. 2 seconds) makes it jerky. Try values between **0.1 and 0.3 seconds**.
Useful looks blocks

head: Block
What it does
rows: Shows a chosen costume, e.g. a 'sad' costume when you lose a life
Moves on to the next costume in the list, then back to the first after the last
Changes the stage's background, e.g. a new level
Makes the sprite bigger or smaller; 100% is normal size
Changes its colour; other effects include ghost (see-through)
Makes the sprite appear or disappear
A thought bubble instead of a speech bubble
blocks.caption: Looks blocks

blocks.text: The **Paint** button in the Costumes tab lets you draw your own costumes, and the **Choose a Costume** library has hundreds ready-made. Right-click a costume and choose *duplicate* to make a copy you can change slightly, such as moving an arm, for a smooth animation.
Sound blocks

head: [start sound (Meow)]
[play sound (Meow) until done]
rows: No: the next block runs while the sound plays
Yes: the next block waits until the sound has finished
Sound effects during action, e.g. a 'pop' when you catch something
Music or speech where things should happen afterwards

blocks.text: You can record your own sounds, choose from the sound library or upload a sound file in the **Sounds** tab. [stop all sounds] and [change volume by (-10)] are in the Sound category too.

blocks.title: Worked example: a Giant's Causeway explorer
blocks.context: Aoife wants her explorer sprite to grow bigger as it walks towards the camera, 5 times, with a footstep sound each time. Which blocks should go inside her loop?
steps: She needs a count-controlled loop: [repeat (5)] (covered fully on the next page).
Inside: [next costume] to animate the legs.
[change size by (10)] so it gets bigger each time.
[start sound (footstep)] so the sound plays while it moves on.
[wait (0.3) seconds] so each step can be seen.
blocks.answer: [repeat (5)] containing [next costume], [change size by (10)], [start sound (footstep)], [wait (0.3) seconds]. The sprite grows from 100% to 150%.

blocks.text: If you [hide] a sprite at the end of a game, remember to put [show] in its green flag script. Otherwise the next time you click the green flag the sprite stays invisible and looks as if it has vanished.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A costume is one picture a sprite can show; a backdrop is a picture for the stage.
Animation = switching costumes quickly, with a short wait between them.
[next costume] cycles through costumes; [switch costume to ()] picks one.
Looks blocks also change size, colour effects, speech and whether a sprite is shown.
[start sound] does not wait; [play sound until done] does.

A script that dresses up a sprite

check.q: A sprite is at size 100%. It runs [change size by (10)] four times. What size is it now?

practice.q: Explain how a sprite can be made to look as if it is walking in Scratch.
practice.a: Use more than one costume showing slightly different leg positions (1); switch between them with [next costume] inside a loop (1); with a short wait between changes and/or move blocks so it moves across (1).

pages.spec: Use repeat, forever and repeat until loops and explain why loops make code shorter
pages.summary: Iteration means repeating blocks using a loop. [repeat (10)] is a count-controlled loop that runs a set number of times; [repeat until <>] is a condition-controlled loop that stops when its condition becomes true; [forever] never stops. Loops make code shorter, easier to read and easier to change.

diagram.title: Draw any regular shape
diagram.caption: Change the number of sides. Inside [repeat (sides)], the sprite does [move (100) steps] then turns by this many degrees.

blocks.text: Imagine drawing a square. Without a loop you need eight blocks: move, turn, move, turn, move, turn, move, turn. You are writing the **same two blocks four times**. A **[[loop]]** lets you write them once and repeat them. Repeating blocks is called **[[iteration]]**.

head: Without a loop
With a loop
rows: Add 4 more blocks and change every turn
Higher: easy to miss one block

blocks.title: Drawing a square with the Pen extension
blocks.code:
[when green flag clicked]
[erase all]
[go to x: (0) y: (0)]
[pen down]
[repeat (4)]
    [move (100) steps]
    [turn ↻ (90) degrees]
[pen up]
blocks.output: A square with sides of 100 steps. The pen blocks come from Add Extension > Pen.

blocks.text: Three kinds of loop

head: Loop
Type
Stops when...
Example use
rows: it has run the set number of times
Walk until you reach the wall
never: only the red stop sign ends it
Keep checking keys in a game, background music
blocks.caption: Loops in Scratch (all in the orange Control category)

blocks.text: Loops are **C-shaped blocks**: the blocks you want to repeat go *inside* the C. Anything placed underneath a [repeat] or [repeat until] runs once the loop has finished. Nothing can go underneath [forever], because it never finishes.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: the right numbers for a shape
blocks.context: Conor wants to draw a regular hexagon (6 equal sides). What should his loop look like?
steps: A full turn is **360 degrees**. The sprite must turn all the way round once while drawing the shape.
Turn angle = 360 / number of sides = 360 / 6 = **60 degrees**.
The loop must run once for each side: **6 times**.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: walk to the edge
blocks.context: A sprite at x = -200 faces right. It runs: [repeat until <touching (edge)?>] containing [move (10) steps]. Then it says 'Made it!'. Explain what happens.
steps: Before each repeat, Scratch checks: is the sprite touching the edge? At the start, **no**, so it moves 10 steps.
It keeps checking and moving: x = -190, -180, -170 and so on.
When it touches the right-hand edge the condition is **true**, so the loop stops.
The next block under the loop runs: it says 'Made it!'.
blocks.answer: The sprite walks right in steps of 10 until it touches the edge, then says 'Made it!'. We did not need to know how many steps it would take.

blocks.text: Choose a **count-controlled** loop when you know how many times before you start (e.g. 4 sides). Choose a **condition-controlled** loop when you do not know how many times, only when to stop (e.g. until the score reaches 10).

In Scratch, [repeat until] stops when its condition becomes **true**. If the condition can never become true (e.g. *until touching Sprite2* when Sprite2 is hidden), the loop never ends and the rest of the script never runs.
Blocks placed *after* a loop run only once, when the loop ends. A common bug is putting [next costume] under a [repeat] instead of inside it, so the costume changes only once.
Loops inside loops

You can put a loop inside another loop. [repeat (3)] containing the square-drawing [repeat (4)] loop, plus [turn ↻ (120) degrees], draws three squares in a fan. The inner loop runs 4 times **for each** of the 3 outer repeats: 12 sides in total.
When you meet C# in Year 10, [repeat (10)] becomes a **for loop** and [repeat until] becomes a **while loop**. The ideas are exactly the same, only the way you write them changes.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Iteration means repeating; a loop repeats the blocks inside it.
[repeat (n)] is count-controlled: it runs a fixed number of times.
[repeat until <condition>] is condition-controlled: it stops when the condition is true.
[forever] is an infinite loop: it only stops when the project is stopped.
Loops make scripts shorter, easier to read and easier to change.
For a regular shape, turn 360 / number of sides degrees.

practice.q: Explain **two** advantages of using a loop instead of copying the same blocks many times.
practice.a: Any two: shorter script / fewer blocks (1); easier to read (1); easier to change, e.g. one number to edit (1); fewer chances of mistakes (1).

practice.q: Describe the difference between a **count-controlled** and a **condition-controlled** loop, giving a Scratch block for each.
practice.a: Count-controlled repeats a set number of times (1), e.g. [repeat (10)] (1). Condition-controlled repeats until a condition is met/true (1), e.g. [repeat until <touching edge?>] (1).

pages.spec: Use if and if-else blocks with sensing blocks so a program can make decisions
pages.summary: Selection lets a program choose what to do. [if <condition> then] runs its blocks only when the condition is true; [if <> then else] picks one of two paths. Sensing blocks such as <touching (Bowl)?>, <key (space) pressed?> and [ask () and wait] give the conditions and inputs, and an if usually needs to sit inside a forever loop so it keeps checking.

diagram.title: Is the cat touching the apple?
diagram.caption: Click each block. Inside a forever loop, the if-else checks again and again.

nodes.label: forever
nodes.detail: Keeps repeating the check, many times a second.

nodes.label: touching Apple?
nodes.detail: A sensing block. Its answer is either true or false.

nodes.label: say Yum! and change score by 1
nodes.detail: Runs only when the condition is true.

nodes.label: say Where is it?
nodes.detail: The else part: runs only when the condition is false.

blocks.text: So far our scripts have done the same thing every time. Real programs **make decisions**: if you catch the apple, your score goes up; if you touch the lava, you lose a life. Choosing between different paths is called **[[selection]]**.
If and if-else

head: [if <> then]
[if <> then else]
rows: One: do something, or do nothing
Two: do one thing or the other
Runs the blocks in the top gap
Runs the blocks in the else gap
If touching lava, lose a life
If answer = 56, say Correct, else say Try again

blocks.text: The **[[condition]]** is the hexagon-shaped (pointy-ended) gap in the if block. Only **[[Boolean]]** blocks fit there: blocks whose answer is always **true** or **false**, such as <touching (edge)?> or <(score) > (10)>.
Sensing blocks
**[[Sensing]]** blocks (light blue) let a sprite find out what is going on: is it touching something, is a key being pressed, where is the mouse?

head: Sensing block
What it reports
rows: True if this sprite is touching the Apple sprite (or the mouse-pointer or edge)
True if it is touching that colour, e.g. the black walls of a maze
True while that key is held down
True while the mouse button is pressed
Shows a box for the user to type into, and waits for them
Holds whatever the user typed in the last ask
How many seconds since the project started or the timer was reset
blocks.caption: Sensing blocks

blocks.title: Steering with the arrow keys
blocks.code:
[when green flag clicked]
[forever]
    [if <key (right arrow) pressed?> then]
        [change x by (10)]
    [if <key (left arrow) pressed?> then]
        [change x by (-10)]
blocks.output: The sprite moves smoothly left and right while the arrow keys are held down.

blocks.text: An if block checks its condition **once**, at the moment it runs. If you put [if <touching (Apple)?> then] straight under the green flag with no loop, Scratch checks once at the start and never again. Put it **inside a [forever] loop** so it keeps checking.
Asking questions

blocks.title: A times-table quiz
blocks.code:
[when green flag clicked]
[ask (What is 7 × 8?) and wait]
[if <(answer) = (56)> then]
    [say (Correct! Well done.) for (2) seconds]
[else]
    [say (Not quite: it is 56.) for (2) seconds]

blocks.title: Worked example: trace the quiz
blocks.context: Use the quiz script above. What does the sprite say if the user types (a) 56, (b) 54, (c) fifty-six?
steps: (a) answer = 56, so the condition <(answer) = (56)> is **true**: it says **Correct! Well done.**
(b) 54 is not equal to 56, so the condition is **false** and the else part runs: **Not quite: it is 56.**
(c) The text *fifty-six* is not the same as the number 56, so the condition is **false**: **Not quite: it is 56.**
blocks.answer: (a) Correct! Well done. (b) and (c) Not quite: it is 56.

blocks.text: Scratch's = block ignores capital letters: <(answer) = (belfast)> is true whether the user types *Belfast*, *BELFAST* or *belfast*. Most text-based languages, including C#, are **not** this forgiving.
When there are more than two choices, put an if-else **inside** the else part of another if-else. For example: if score > 20 say *Gold*, else (if score > 10 say *Silver*, else say *Bronze*).

blocks.title: Key points
items: Selection means the program chooses which blocks to run.
[if <> then] has one path; [if <> then else] has two.
A condition is a Boolean: it is always true or false.
Sensing blocks report touching, key presses, the mouse, the timer and typed answers.
Put an if inside a forever loop so it keeps checking.
[ask () and wait] stores what the user types in (answer).

check.q: What does selection allow a program to do?
o: Repeat blocks many times
Run blocks one after another
Choose which blocks to run
Send a message to other sprites
check.why: Selection = making a decision between paths.

check.q: Which kind of block fits in the condition gap of an if block?
o: A hat block such as when flag clicked
A true/false (Boolean) block
A motion block such as move 10 steps
A C-shaped loop block
check.why: Conditions must be Boolean: true or false.

check.q: A pupil's [if <touching (Apple)?> then] is directly under the green flag with no loop. What happens?
o: It is checked only once, at the start
It is checked again and again forever
Scratch will not let the blocks join
It is checked only when the apple moves
check.why: Without a loop the if runs once; put it inside forever.

check.q: Where is the text the user types after [ask () and wait] stored?
o: In the (timer) block
In the (x position) block
In the [say] block
In the (answer) block
check.why: Answer holds the most recent reply.

practice.q: Explain the difference between [if <> then] and [if <> then else].
practice.a: If then only runs its blocks when the condition is true, otherwise nothing happens (1). If-else runs one set of blocks if true and a different set if false (1).

practice.q: Write a script that asks 'What is the capital of Northern Ireland?' and says 'Correct' if the answer is Belfast, or 'Wrong' otherwise.
practice.a: [ask (What is the capital of Northern Ireland?) and wait] (1); [if <(answer) = (Belfast)> then] say Correct (1); else say Wrong (1).

practice.q: Explain why an [if <touching (Lava)?> then] block in a game is usually placed inside a [forever] loop.
practice.a: An if only checks its condition once when it runs (1); the forever loop makes it check continuously so it notices whenever the sprite touches the lava (1).

pages.spec: Create and use variables for score, lives and timers, know the data types they hold, and use operators for maths, comparisons and random numbers
pages.summary: A variable is a named store for a value that can change, such as score, lives or time. In Scratch a variable can hold a number, text (a string) or true/false (a Boolean). Operator blocks do maths (+, -, ×, /), compare values (<, =, >), join text and pick random numbers.

diagram.title: Which operator?
diagram.caption: Match each operator block to what it gives.

blocks.text: Games need to **remember** things: your score, how many lives you have left, how much time is left. A **[[variable]]** is a named store in the computer's memory that holds one value, and that value can **change** (vary) while the program runs.
Making and using a variable

items: Go to the **Variables** category and click **Make a Variable**.
Give it a clear name, such as *score* (not *v1*).
Choose **For all sprites** (every sprite can use it) or **For this sprite only**.
Tick the box beside it to show it on the stage, so the player can see their score.

head: Block
What it does
Example
rows: Puts an exact value in the variable, replacing what was there
Reset the score at the start of a game
Adds to the value (use a negative number to take away)
+1 for each apple caught; [change (lives) by (-1)] when hit
The rounded reporter block: gives the current value
[say (score)], or use it in a condition
Shows or hides the variable on the stage
Hide the timer on the title screen
blocks.caption: Variable blocks

blocks.text: Always **[set]** your variables at the start of the green flag script, e.g. [set (score) to (0)] and [set (lives) to (3)]. If you forget, the score carries on from the last game, so a new game might start with 17 points.
What can a variable hold? Data types
The kind of value stored is called its **[[data type]]**. Scratch quietly works this out for you, but text-based languages like C# make you choose, so it is worth knowing them now.

head: Data type
What it holds
Scratch example
rows: gameOver = false; <(lives) = (0)> reports true or false
blocks.caption: Data types

blocks.text: Operators
**[[Operators|Operator]]** are the green blocks. They take values, do something with them and report the result.

head: Kind
Blocks
Gives
rows: A number. * means multiply, / means divide.
A whole number from 1 to 10, including both 1 and 10
blocks.caption: Operator blocks

blocks.text: Scratch has no 'greater than or equal to' block. To check *score is 10 or more*, use <(score) > (9)> for whole numbers, or <<(score) > (10)> or <(score) = (10)>>.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: trace the variables
blocks.context: A game runs these blocks in order: [set (score) to (0)], [set (lives) to (3)], [change (score) by (5)], [change (lives) by (-1)], [change (score) by (5)], [set (score) to ((score) * (2))]. What are score and lives at the end?
steps: set score to 0, set lives to 3: **score 0, lives 3**.
change score by 5: **score 5**.
change lives by -1: **lives 2**.
change score by 5: **score 10**.
set score to score × 2: 10 × 2 = **20**.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: a countdown timer
blocks.context: A catch game should last 30 seconds. How can a variable called *time* count down and end the game?
steps: [set (time) to (30)] at the start.
[repeat until <(time) = (0)>] containing [wait (1) seconds] and [change (time) by (-1)].
After the loop: [say (Time's up!)] and [stop (all)].
The loop runs 30 times, once a second, so it lasts 30 seconds.
blocks.answer: time goes 30, 29, 28 ... 0, then the game ends.

blocks.text: Scratch also has a built-in **(timer)** in Sensing that counts up in seconds, and [reset timer] sets it back to 0. A variable gives you more control, such as counting down or adding bonus time.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A variable is a named store for a value that can change.
[set] gives a variable an exact value; [change] adds to it.
Reset variables at the start of every game.
Data types: integer, float, string (text) and Boolean (true/false).
Operators do maths, compare values, join text and pick random numbers.
(pick random (1) to (6)) includes both 1 and 6.

check.q: What is a variable?
o: A named store for a value that can change
A block that starts a script
A picture a sprite can show
A loop that never stops

check.q: score is 4. The program runs [change (score) by (3)] then [set (score) to (10)]. What is score now?
check.why: Set replaces whatever was there, so the final value is 10.

check.q: Which data type would store the value true or false?
o: Boolean
String
Integer
Float
check.why: Booleans hold only true or false.

check.q: Which numbers can (pick random (1) to (6)) give?
o: Any whole number from 1 to 5
Any whole number from 2 to 5
Only the numbers 1 and 6
Any whole number from 1 to 6
check.why: Both ends are included, like rolling a dice.

check.q: A game starts with 17 points instead of 0. What is the most likely bug?
o: The score was changed by -1 by mistake
The score was not set to 0 at the start
The score was set to 0 every time
The variable was hidden on the stage
check.why: Without [set (score) to (0)] the old value carries over.

practice.q: Explain what a **variable** is and give **one** example of a variable you might use in a game.
practice.a: A named storage location / value in memory that can change while the program runs (1). e.g. score, lives, time, level (1).

practice.q: State the most suitable data type for: (a) the player's name (b) number of lives (c) whether the game is over.
practice.a: (a) String / text (1). (b) Integer (1). (c) Boolean (1).

pages.spec: Use broadcast and when I receive blocks to send messages between sprites and the stage
pages.summary: A broadcast sends a message to every sprite and the stage. Any script that starts with [when I receive (message)] then runs. Broadcasts let sprites work together, such as starting a level, showing a game-over screen or making one sprite react to another.

diagram.title: A game told by messages
diagram.caption: Click each step to see which sprite broadcasts and who receives.

items.label: Green flag: title screen
items.detail: The stage shows the title backdrop. The Start button sprite shows itself.

items.label: Start clicked: broadcast start game
items.detail: The Start button hides, then broadcasts start game.

items.label: Everyone receives start game
items.detail: The stage switches backdrop, the apple starts falling, the bowl can move and the timer starts.

items.label: Lives reach 0: broadcast game over
items.detail: The apple sprite spots lives = 0 and broadcasts game over.

items.label: Everyone receives game over
items.detail: The stage shows the Game Over backdrop, the bowl hides and the music stops.

blocks.text: In a real game, lots of sprites need to work **together**. When the player clicks *Start*, the title must disappear, the music start and the enemies begin moving. How does the Start button tell everyone else? It sends a **[[broadcast]]**.
How broadcasting works

head: Block
Category
What it does
rows: Sends the message *start game* to every sprite and the stage, then carries straight on
Sends the message, then waits until every script that received it has finished
A hat block: starts this script whenever that message is broadcast
blocks.caption: Broadcast blocks

blocks.text: Think of a broadcast like the **school intercom**. The office makes one announcement and it goes to every classroom. Each class decides what to do when it hears it, and classes it does not concern simply ignore it.
Create a new message by clicking the drop-down arrow on a broadcast block and choosing **New message**. Give it a clear name such as *game over* or *level 2*, not *message1*.

blocks.title: Start button sprite
blocks.code:
[when green flag clicked]
[show]

[when this sprite clicked]
[hide]
[broadcast (start game)]

blocks.title: Stage
blocks.code:
[when I receive (start game)]
[switch backdrop to (Lough Erne)]
[start sound (music)]

blocks.title: Apple sprite
blocks.code:
[when I receive (start game)]
[show]
[go to x: (pick random (-220) to (220)) y: (170)]
[forever]
    [change y by (-5)]

blocks.title: Worked example: who does what?
blocks.context: In a quiz game, the Teacher sprite asks a question. If the answer is right, the Teacher broadcasts *correct*. The Crowd sprite has [when I receive (correct)] then [play sound (cheer) until done]. The Score sprite has [when I receive (correct)] then [change (score) by (1)]. What happens when the user answers correctly?
steps: The Teacher's if block is true, so it runs [broadcast (correct)].
Every sprite gets the message. The Crowd's receive script starts: it **cheers**.
At the same time, the Score sprite's receive script starts: **score goes up by 1**.
Any sprite without a [when I receive (correct)] script does nothing.
blocks.answer: One broadcast makes two different sprites react at the same time: the crowd cheers and the score increases.

blocks.text: Broadcast names must match **exactly**. If one sprite broadcasts *game over* and another is waiting for *gameover*, nothing happens. Use the drop-down to pick an existing message instead of making a new one with a slightly different name.
Do not put [broadcast] inside a [forever] loop without an if around it. It would send the message over and over many times a second, restarting the receiving scripts so they never get to finish.
Broadcasts are a simple way of passing **control** from one part of a program to another. Larger programs use similar ideas: buttons on a website send *events*, and code elsewhere listens for them.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A broadcast sends a message to every sprite and the stage.
[when I receive (message)] starts a script when that message arrives.
Broadcasts let sprites work together, e.g. start game, level up, game over.
[broadcast and wait] waits until the receiving scripts finish.
Message names must match exactly; give them clear names.

Only the sprite touching the sender
Only the stage
Every sprite and the stage
check.why: Broadcasts go to everyone; only scripts with a matching receive block react.

check.q: Which block starts a script when a message arrives?
o: [when I receive (message)]
[broadcast (message)]
[when this sprite clicked]
[wait until <>]
check.why: When I receive is the hat block for messages.

check.q: Sprite A broadcasts 'game over'. Sprite B has [when I receive (gameover)]. What happens?
o: Sprite B runs its script as normal
Scratch shows an error message
Nothing, because the names do not match
Sprite A runs sprite B's script
check.why: Message names must match exactly.

check.q: How is [broadcast (level 2) and wait] different from [broadcast (level 2)]?
o: It only sends to one chosen sprite
It waits for the receiving scripts to finish
It waits two seconds before sending
It repeats the message every second
check.why: The 'and wait' version pauses until all receiving scripts end.

practice.q: Explain what a **broadcast** is in Scratch and why it is useful.
practice.a: A message sent to all sprites and the stage (1); lets sprites communicate/work together, e.g. starting a level or game over (1).

practice.q: A Start button should hide and make the stage change to the 'Level 1' backdrop. Write the scripts for the button and the stage.

pages.spec: Use abstraction to reduce complexity by making My Blocks (custom blocks) with inputs
pages.summary: A My Block is a custom block you define once and then use whenever you need it, giving a long set of blocks a single clear name. This is abstraction: hiding detail you do not need to think about. Inputs (parameters) let the same block do slightly different jobs, such as drawing a shape with any number of sides.

diagram.title: Without and with a My Block
diagram.caption: The same drawing of a hexagon, a square and a triangle, written two ways.

states.label: Without My Blocks
points: Three separate repeat loops written out in full
Every move and turn typed in each time
Hard to see at a glance what the script draws
A change to the size means editing every loop

states.label: With a My Block
points: Main script: draw shape (6) (50), draw shape (4) (80), draw shape (3) (100)
Change the definition once and every shape updates

blocks.text: As projects grow, scripts get long and hard to follow. Programmers deal with this using **[[abstraction]]**: hiding the details you do not need right now, and giving a group of instructions a simple name. You already use abstraction every day: you say *make toast* rather than listing every step of using the toaster.
My Blocks: make your own block

In the pink **My Blocks** category, click **Make a Block**. You name your new block and Scratch gives you a **define** hat block. The blocks you put under *define* are what your new block does. This is called a **[[custom block|My Block]]**.

blocks.title: A My Block with no inputs
blocks.code:
[define jump]
[repeat (10)]
    [change y by (10)]
[repeat (10)]
    [change y by (-10)]

[when (space) key pressed]
[jump]
blocks.output: Pressing space makes the sprite jump up 100 steps and back down. The space-key script only needs one block.

blocks.text: Inputs make blocks more useful

When you make a block you can **add an input**: a number or text box that the user of the block fills in. Inside the define script, the input appears as a round block you can drag into other blocks. In text-based languages like C# these inputs are called **[[parameters|Parameter]]**, and the custom block itself is called a **function** (or method).

blocks.title: A My Block with two inputs
blocks.code:
[define draw shape (sides) (size)]
[pen down]
[repeat (sides)]
    [move (size) steps]
    [turn ↻ ((360) / (sides)) degrees]
[pen up]

[when green flag clicked]
[erase all]
[draw shape (6) (50)]
[draw shape (4) (80)]
[draw shape (3) (100)]
blocks.output: A hexagon with sides of 50, a square with sides of 80 and a triangle with sides of 100, all from one definition.

blocks.title: Worked example: using inputs
blocks.context: Using the *draw shape* block above, what is drawn by [draw shape (8) (40)], and what turn does the sprite make?
steps: sides = 8 and size = 40.
The loop repeats 8 times, moving 40 steps each time.
The turn is 360 / sides = 360 / 8 = **45 degrees**.
blocks.answer: A regular octagon with sides of 40 steps, turning 45 degrees at each corner.

blocks.text: Why bother?

items: **Shorter, tidier scripts**: the main script reads like a list of jobs.
**Less repetition**: write the details once, use them many times.
**Easier to fix**: a bug in *draw shape* is fixed in one place and every shape is fixed.
**Easier to share work**: one person can build *jump* while another builds the scoring, as long as they agree what each block does.

blocks.text: A My Block belongs to the sprite it was made in. If you make *jump* on the Cat, the Dog sprite cannot use it unless you make it again there (or drag the define script on to the Dog in the sprite list to copy it).
Give My Blocks **verb names** that say what they do: *draw shape*, *reset game*, *lose a life*. Then your main script explains itself.
New NI curriculum link: **abstraction to reduce complexity**, and My Blocks with inputs lead straight on to **functions and parameters** in text-based code.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Abstraction means hiding detail and giving a set of instructions a simple name.
A My Block is a custom block: define it once, use it many times.
Inputs (parameters) let one block do slightly different jobs.
My Blocks make scripts shorter, clearer and easier to fix.
In text-based languages, My Blocks are called functions and inputs are called parameters.

Sending a message to every sprite
Hiding detail and giving instructions a simple name

pages.spec: Use variables to build a simple simulation, and explain how changing a variable changes the outcome of a model
pages.summary: A model is a simplified version of a real system, and a simulation runs the model to see what happens. In Scratch, variables such as gravity, bounciness or growth rate control the model: change one and you can test a prediction, such as how quickly rabbits fill an island or how high a ball bounces.

diagram.title: Rabbit island simulation
diagram.caption: Change the starting rabbits, the growth each year and the number of years. This is what the Scratch population model calculates.

blocks.text: Engineers, scientists and game designers often need to answer *what if?* questions before building anything. What if a bridge has to carry twice the traffic? What if a disease spreads faster? They build a **[[model]]**: a **simplified** version of the real thing that keeps only the parts that matter. Running the model to see what happens over time is a **[[simulation]]**.

Models leave things out on purpose. A model of rabbits on an island might ignore weather, foxes and illness. That makes it easier to build, but it also means its predictions are **only as good as the model**.
Simulation 1: a bouncing ball

Real balls speed up as they fall, because of gravity, and lose some height with every bounce. We can model that with two variables: **speed** (how fast the ball is moving up or down) and **gravity** (how much the speed changes every moment).

blocks.title: Ball sprite
blocks.code:
[when green flag clicked]
[go to x: (0) y: (150)]
[set (speed) to (0)]
[set (gravity) to (-1)]
[forever]
    [change (speed) by (gravity)]
    [change y by (speed)]
    [if <(y position) < (-150)> then]
        [set y to (-150)]
        [set (speed) to ((speed) * (-0.8))]
blocks.output: The ball falls faster and faster, bounces, and each bounce is lower than the last until it settles on the ground.

head: Variable
What it represents
Try changing it to...
What happens
rows: Floaty falling, like on the Moon
Bounciness: how much speed is kept
A super-bouncy ball that keeps bouncing high
A dead ball that barely bounces, like a beanbag
blocks.caption: Changing variables changes the outcome

blocks.text: Make sliders: right-click a variable shown on the stage and choose **slider**. Now you can change gravity while the simulation is running and watch the effect straight away.
Simulation 2: rabbits on an island

blocks.title: Stage
blocks.code:
[when green flag clicked]
[set (rabbits) to (20)]
[set (year) to (0)]
[repeat (4)]
    [wait (1) seconds]
    [change (year) by (1)]
    [set (rabbits) to ((rabbits) * (1.5))]
    [say (join (Year ) (year))]
blocks.output: Each year the number of rabbits grows by 50%.

blocks.title: Worked example: run the model by hand
blocks.context: Start with 20 rabbits. Each year the population is multiplied by 1.5 (a 50% increase). How many rabbits are there after 4 years?
steps: Year 3: 45 × 1.5 = **67.5** (about 68 rabbits).
blocks.answer: About 101 rabbits after 4 years: the population has roughly multiplied by 5.

blocks.title: Worked example: test a prediction
blocks.context: Ciara predicts: 'If the growth rate is doubled from 50% to 100%, there will be twice as many rabbits after 4 years.' Use the model to test her prediction.
steps: At 100% growth the population doubles each year: 20, 40, 80, 160, **320**.
At 50% growth there were about **101**.
320 is more than three times 101, not twice.
blocks.answer: Her prediction is wrong: the model shows about 320 rabbits, over three times as many, because the growth builds on itself each year.

blocks.text: A simulation is not the real world. Real rabbits run out of food and space, so a real population would not keep growing for ever. Always ask: **what has this model left out**, and could that change the answer?

New NI curriculum link: **a model is a simplified representation of a real system; changing variables changes outcomes; simulations use models to test predictions.** Weather forecasts, flight simulators and video game physics all work this way.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A model is a simplified version of a real system.
A simulation runs a model to see what happens over time.
Variables such as gravity or growth rate control the model.
Changing a variable lets you test a 'what if?' prediction.
Models leave things out, so their predictions can be wrong.

A simplified version of a real system
A picture used as a sprite costume
A list of every block in a script

practice.a: A model is a simplified representation of a real system (1). A simulation runs/uses the model to see what happens over time or to test predictions (1).

pages.spec: Find and fix bugs by tracing a script and recognising common Scratch errors
pages.summary: A bug is a mistake that stops a program doing what it should; debugging is finding and fixing it. Scratch blocks stop most typing errors, so most Scratch bugs are logic errors: blocks in the wrong order, the wrong sprite, set instead of change, a missing loop or reset, or a condition that is never true. Tracing a script step by step shows where it goes wrong.

lives

blocks.text: Every programmer, from Year 8 pupils to the engineers at Belfast's software companies, writes **[[bugs|Bug]]**. A bug is a mistake that makes a program do the wrong thing. **[[Debugging]]** means finding the bug and fixing it. Good programmers are not people who never make mistakes; they are people who are good at finding them.
Logic errors

In text-based languages, many bugs are **syntax errors**: a spelling mistake or a missing bracket that stops the code running at all. Scratch blocks only fit together correctly, so syntax errors are almost impossible. Instead, Scratch bugs are usually **[[logic errors|Logic error]]**: the program runs, but does the wrong thing.
Tracing a script

**Tracing** means stepping through a script one block at a time, writing down what happens to each variable and sprite, just as the computer would. It works best on paper, or by clicking blocks one at a time in the scripts area to see what each one does.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: trace and find the bug
blocks.context: This script should make the cat count up from 1 to 5: [set (count) to (0)], [repeat (5)] containing [say (count) for (1) seconds] and [change (count) by (1)]. The cat says 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Find and fix the bug.
steps: Trace: count = 0. Loop 1: says **0**, then count becomes 1.
Loop 2: says 1, count becomes 2. Loop 3: says 2. Loop 4: says 3. Loop 5: says 4, count becomes 5.
The say block runs **before** the change block, so each number is said before it goes up.
Fix: swap the two blocks inside the loop (change first, then say), or start count at 1.
blocks.answer: It is a sequence bug. With [change (count) by (1)] above [say (count) for (1) seconds], the cat says 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

blocks.text: Common Scratch bugs

head: Symptom
Likely cause
Fix
rows: Nothing happens when the flag is clicked
No hat block, or the script is on the wrong sprite
Add [when green flag clicked]; check which sprite is selected

blocks.title: Worked example 2: off by a little
blocks.context: A game should end when score reaches 10. The script uses [repeat until <(score) = (10)>]. Each apple is worth 3 points. Why does the game never end?
steps: score is never exactly 10, so <(score) = (10)> is never true.
The repeat until loop never stops.
blocks.answer: Use <(score) > (9)> so the game ends once the score is 10 or more (it will end at 12).

blocks.text: Debugging tricks: **click a single block** to run it on its own; **show variables** on the stage so you can watch them change; add a temporary [say (score)] to see a value; add [wait (1) seconds] to slow things down so you can see what is happening.
Change **one thing at a time**, then test again. If you change five blocks at once and it works (or breaks), you will not know which change made the difference.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A bug is an error in a program; debugging is finding and fixing it.
Scratch bugs are mostly logic errors: the program runs but does the wrong thing.
Tracing means stepping through a script block by block, tracking the variables.
Common bugs: wrong order, wrong sprite, set instead of change, missing reset, if not in a loop.
Change one thing at a time and test after each change.

check.q: What is debugging?
o: Adding new sprites to a project
Deleting all of the scripts
Making a program run faster
Finding and fixing errors in a program
check.why: A bug is an error; debugging removes it.

check.q: Why are syntax errors rare in Scratch?
o: Blocks only fit together in ways that make sense
Scratch fixes every mistake for you
Scratch programs are always very short
Scratch has no variables or loops
check.why: Block shapes stop most spelling and bracket mistakes.

check.q: A script says [set (n) to (2)], [repeat (3)] containing [change (n) by (2)]. What is n at the end?
A sprite should move right each time the arrow key is pressed but stays in one spot. Which bug is most likely?
o: [change x by (10)] used instead of [set x to (10)]
The sprite's costume is the wrong colour
[set x to (10)] used instead of [change x by (10)]
The backdrop has not been changed
check.why: Set always puts it at the same position.

check.q: Score goes up in 4s. Why does [repeat until <(score) = (10)>] never stop?
o: Repeat until loops can only run 10 times
Score goes 8 then 12 and is never exactly 10
A score of 10 is too large for a variable
The = block only works with text values
check.why: The condition is never true, so the loop never ends.

practice.q: State what is meant by a **logic error** and give an example from Scratch.
practice.a: An error where the program runs but does not do what was intended / gives the wrong result (1). e.g. blocks in the wrong order, set instead of change, wrong condition (1).

practice.q: A pupil's game always starts with the score from the previous game. Explain the cause and how to fix it.
practice.a: The score variable is not reset at the start (1). Add [set (score) to (0)] under [when green flag clicked] (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** techniques a programmer could use to find a bug in a Scratch project.
practice.a: Any two: trace the script on paper (1); click blocks one at a time (1); show variables on the stage / add say blocks to display values (1); add waits to slow it down (1); change one thing at a time and retest (1).

pages.spec: Plan, develop, test and refine a simple game for a user, using a user story and a test table
pages.summary: Software is made in cycles: plan, develop, test and refine, then go round again. Start by asking who the game is for and writing a user story ('As a ... I want ... so that ...'). Build one feature at a time, test each one with a test table of normal, boundary and erroneous tests, and refine it using what you find and what users say.

diagram.title: The development cycle
diagram.caption: Go round the cycle once for each feature, not just once for the whole game.

items.label: Plan
items.detail: Who is it for? Write a user story, sketch the screen, list the sprites, variables and messages.

items.label: Develop
items.detail: Build one small feature, e.g. moving the bowl with the arrow keys.

items.label: Test
items.detail: Use a test table: what should happen, what did happen, pass or fail?

items.label: Refine
items.detail: Fix bugs and improve it using test results and feedback from real users, then plan the next feature.

blocks.text: Games are not made in one go. Professional developers, including games studios in Belfast, work in **cycles**: they plan a little, build a little, test it and improve it, then go round again. This is called **[[iterative development]]**, and you should make your Scratch games the same way.
Step 1: plan for a real user

Before building anything, ask **who is this game for?** A game for a five-year-old cousin needs big buttons, simple controls and no reading; a game for your form class can be faster and harder. Designing around the people who will use it is called **user-centred design**.
A **[[user story]]** sums up what a user needs in one sentence: **As a** (type of user) **I want** (something) **so that** (reason).

head: User story
What it tells the designer
rows: As a **Year 8 pupil with five minutes at break**, I want **a quick game with a score** so that **I can try to beat my friends**.
Short games, a clear score on screen, an easy restart
As a **P2 pupil who is still learning to read**, I want **picture instructions** so that **I know what to do without help**.
Few words, big pictures, simple controls
As a **player who is colour-blind**, I want **the good and bad items to be different shapes** so that **I can tell them apart**.
Do not rely on colour alone
blocks.caption: User stories for a catch game

blocks.text: Our game: Orchard Catch

Armagh is the Orchard County, so our game has apples falling from the top of the stage. The player moves a basket with the arrow keys. Catch an apple: +1 point. Miss one: lose a life. Three lives; the game lasts 30 seconds.

head: Plan item
Our game
rows: A My Block *reset apple* that sends the apple to a random x at the top

[go to x: (pick random (-220) to (220)) y: (170)]

blocks.text: Step 3: test with a test table

A **[[test table]]** lists each test, the **expected result** (what should happen) and the **actual result** (what did happen). Good testing uses three kinds of **[[test data]]**: **normal** (what you expect a player to do), **boundary** (right at the edges, such as the last life or the edge of the stage) and **erroneous** (things a player should not do, such as pressing the wrong key).

blocks.title: Worked example: refine using the test results
blocks.context: Tests 4 and 7 failed. Suggest the cause of each and a fix.
steps: **Test 4**: the apple broadcasts *game over*, but the Game Over sprite is waiting for *gameover*. The names do not match, so nothing receives it. Fix: choose the same message from the drop-down.
**Test 7**: the apple hides at the end and the green flag script was missing [show]. Fix: add [show] near the top of the green flag script (as in the script above).
Then **re-run every test**, not just the ones that failed, in case a fix broke something else.
blocks.answer: Fix the message name and add [show], then retest everything.

blocks.text: Refining is not only fixing bugs. Watch someone from your user story play it: is it too fast? Are the instructions clear? Each answer becomes the plan for your next trip round the cycle, such as adding a *speed up every 5 points* feature.
New NI curriculum link: **software development follows cycles of planning, development, testing and refinement**, and **user stories** help plan products that meet real users' needs.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Develop in cycles: plan, develop, test, refine, then repeat.
Start with who the game is for; write a user story: As a ... I want ... so that ...
Build and test one feature at a time.
A test table records each test, expected result, actual result and pass/fail.
Use normal, boundary and erroneous test data.
After a fix, retest everything.

check.q: What are the four stages of the development cycle in order?
o: Plan, develop, test, refine
Develop, plan, refine, test
Test, plan, develop, refine
Plan, test, develop, refine
check.why: Plan first, then build, then test, then improve, and go round again.

check.q: Which is written as a user story?
o: The game has three lives and a 30 second timer
As a Year 7 pupil I want big buttons so that I can play easily
Test 4 failed because the message names did not match
The apple falls 5 steps at a time from the top
check.why: User stories follow As a ... I want ... so that ...

check.q: In a test table, what is the expected result?
o: What should happen if the program works
What actually happened in the test
Whether the test passed or failed
The kind of data used in the test
check.why: Expected = what should happen; actual = what did happen.

check.q: A game has 3 lives. Which is boundary test data?
o: Catching one apple
Pressing the space bar
Losing the last life
Moving the basket left
check.why: Boundary tests are at the edge of what is allowed, e.g. the final life.

check.q: After fixing a bug, what should you do?
o: Only retest the one test that failed
Delete the test table as it is finished
Move on, as fixes never cause new bugs
Retest all the tests, not just the failed one
check.why: A fix can break something else, so retest everything.

practice.q: Write a **user story** for a Scratch maths quiz game for P6 pupils.
practice.a: Correct format As a ... I want ... so that ... (1); sensible content linked to P6 pupils' needs, e.g. As a P6 pupil I want the quiz to tell me the right answer when I get it wrong so that I can learn from mistakes (1).

practice.q: Describe the **four** stages of the development cycle.
practice.a: Plan: decide what to make, who it is for, design (1). Develop: build/code a feature (1). Test: check it works using a test table (1). Refine: fix bugs/improve using results and feedback, then repeat (1).

practice.q: A catch game ends when lives reach 0. Give **one** normal, **one** boundary and **one** erroneous test for this game, with the expected result for each.
practice.a: Normal, e.g. miss an apple with 3 lives: lives becomes 2 (1). Boundary, e.g. miss with 1 life left: lives 0 and game over (1). Erroneous, e.g. press a key not used: nothing happens (1).

glossary.def: A free, block-based programming language from the MIT Media Lab. Programs are built by snapping blocks together.
A character or object on the stage that can be programmed with its own scripts, e.g. the Scratch Cat.
The area of the Scratch window where the project runs. It is 480 steps wide and 360 steps tall.
A background picture for the stage. Switching backdrops can show a new level or screen.
The part of the Scratch window that lists the blocks in the chosen category, ready to drag.
A stack of joined blocks that runs from top to bottom, usually started by a hat block.
Something that happens, such as clicking the green flag or pressing a key, that starts a script.
Carrying out instructions one after another, in order. A Scratch script runs from top to bottom.
A pair of numbers (x, y) giving an exact position on the stage. The centre is (0, 0).
One of the pictures a sprite can show. Switching costumes changes how the sprite looks.
A block that repeats the blocks inside it, such as [repeat (10)], [repeat until] or [forever].
Repeating a set of instructions using a loop.
A loop that repeats a set number of times, known before it starts, e.g. [repeat (4)].
A loop that repeats until a condition becomes true, e.g. [repeat until <touching (edge)?>].
Choosing which instructions to run depending on a condition, using if or if-else blocks.
A test whose answer is either true or false, e.g. <(score) > (10)>.
A value or block that can only be true or false. Boolean blocks have pointed (hexagon) ends.
Scratch blocks that find out what is happening, such as touching, key pressed, mouse position, timer and ask/answer.
A named store in memory that holds a value which can change while the program runs, e.g. score.
The kind of value stored, such as integer, float, string (text) or Boolean (true/false).
A block or symbol that does something with values: maths (+ - * /), comparisons or joining text.
An operator that compares two values and gives true or false: <, = or >.
A message sent to every sprite and the stage; scripts with a matching [when I receive] block then start.
Hiding detail that is not needed and giving a set of instructions a simple name, to reduce complexity.
A custom block you define yourself in the My Blocks category and can use as often as you like.
An input to a custom block or function that lets it do slightly different jobs, e.g. the number of sides.
A simplified representation of a real system that keeps only the parts that matter.
Running a model to see what happens over time or to test a prediction.
An error in a program that stops it working as it should.
Finding and fixing bugs in a program.
An error where the program runs but does the wrong thing, e.g. blocks in the wrong order.
Making software in repeated cycles of planning, developing, testing and refining.
A short sentence describing what a user needs: As a ... I want ... so that ...
A table listing each test with its expected result, actual result and whether it passed.
Values or actions used to test a program: normal, boundary and erroneous.
